What You Work On

PowerSync Offline Sync & Data Replication ~11 sessions
Extensive debugging of PowerSync's handling of non-_id ObjectId fields being replicated as null, plus per-org zero-row sync failures. Claude diagnosed connector and Atlas trigger issues, implemented orgKey string-denormalization workarounds, and validated sync-streams.yaml configs, though many fixes remained partially working at session end. Heavy iterative deploy-relaunch-log cycles characterized this challenging area.
Offline-First Desktop Architecture ~8 sessions
Building local-first, offline-capable behavior into a pharmacy/POS desktop app, including offline detection, settings persistence, and a multi-phase local-first architecture wired to entity writes. Claude orchestrated parallel agents and restored 43 missing locale keys as part of the effort. Work often built cleanly but ended mid-task while wiring writes or awaiting external PowerSync deployment.
Electron/Tauri Desktop Packaging & Distribution ~6 sessions
Fixing packaged desktop app startup crashes (traced to unresolved pnpm symlinks), adding electron-forge auto-updates with S3, version bumping, app branding, and icon shipping. Claude also planned migration of a Next.js website into Tauri and Electron POS apps. Configuration mismatches between electron-builder and forge occasionally required reconciliation.
Feature Implementation & UI Redesign ~7 sessions
Implementing supplier features (manual credit, marketplace dashboard), a persistent POS side-drawer via iframe, marketplace email notifications, per-user AI key replacement, and bilingual SEO. Claude also redesigned dashboards as shared components across two apps while preserving data wiring. Delivered via multi-file edits with clean typechecks, though some work went uncommitted or hit usage limits.
Bug Fixing & Localization ~5 sessions
Parallel sub-agent bug-fixing across three apps (25+ bugs fixed with worktree cleanup), i18n reviews, git reflog recovery of forge migration work, and API rewrite/404 fixes for sync endpoints. Claude also resolved localization collisions and bar-overflow rendering bugs across locale files. Strong debugging performance with mostly verified outcomes.

How You Use Claude Code

You operate as a technical architect running long, ambitious engineering campaigns—110 hours across 34 sessions building offline-first pharmacy/POS systems, PowerSync integrations, and Electron desktop apps. Your defining trait is delegating large, complex missions and letting Claude run autonomously, often orchestrating parallel sub-agents and worktrees (the Agent tool appears 332 times) to 'fix all remaining bugs across three apps' or 'complete the final Wave A3 ticket.' You think in phased plans and gated deliverables, expecting Claude to explore the codebase, produce specs, and verify with clean typechecks before you consider work done. This is a high-trust, high-ambition style: you hand off whole architectural layers (a 5-phase local-first migration) rather than dictating line-by-line edits.

Despite the autonomy, you stay actively engaged and interrupt decisively when Claude drifts off-course. Multiple sessions show you interrupting a standalone build twice until Claude chained it into a package.json script, redirecting an approach mid-tool-call, or cutting off a brainstorming dialogue before it produced the plan you didn't want. Your friction is dominated by wrong_approach (12) and buggy_code (14)—not misunderstanding—which signals you're less bothered by Claude misreading you than by Claude taking too long to root-cause. The grueling PowerSync null-ObjectId saga is the archetype: you tolerated many deploy-relaunch-log iterations, but frustration surfaced when Claude cycled through blame theories before isolating the real cause.

You favor verification-driven, correctness-obsessed delivery over quick prototyping—you repeatedly ask Claude to confirm nothing was lost (via git reflog), validate config against live docs, and cross-check for demo data. Your outcomes cluster in 'mostly/partially achieved' not because Claude misfires, but because your targets are deep systems problems that often bottom out in external blockers (undeployed PowerSync streams, Meta blocking WhatsApp in Syria, stale Windows dev bundles). You accept partial wins gracefully and frequently take over environment-level fixes yourself, treating Claude as a capable senior collaborator on shared, genuinely hard problems.

Key pattern: You delegate ambitious multi-phase engineering campaigns to autonomous (often parallel-agent) execution, then interrupt decisively to redirect approach while demanding rigorous verification.

Impressive Things You Did

Over 110 hours across 34 sessions, you tackled deep full-stack debugging and ambitious feature work on your pharmacy POS ecosystem—spanning Next.js, Electron, Tauri, PowerSync, and multi-app monorepos.

Orchestrated parallel agent builds
You leaned heavily on the Agent tool (332 uses) to run parallel sub-agents across worktrees—auditing and fixing 25+ bugs across three apps, then merging and cleaning up worktrees with no lingering state. You used lane-ownership boundaries and Grep verification to ensure parallel agents didn't clobber each other's files, turning complex multi-app work into coordinated, gated deliveries.
Systematic root-cause debugging
Your debugging sessions (14 of them, backed by strong good-debugging signals) consistently isolated tricky root causes—like PowerSync replicating non-_id ObjectId fields as null, unresolved pnpm symlinks breaking packaged builds, and a sync-config table-name mismatch that unlocked 23k rows. You favored deploy-relaunch-log iteration loops and cross-checked configs against live docs and schemas rather than guessing.
Spec-first feature planning
Before implementing big changes—like the Tauri desktop wrapper, offline-first Electron migration, or the persistent POS side-drawer—you had Claude write specs and phased implementation plans first, often catching fatal blockers early (Meta blocking WhatsApp delivery to Syria, static-export incompatibility). This planning discipline let you ship shared-component dashboard redesigns and multi-phase local-first architectures with clean typechecks.

Where Things Go Wrong

Your sessions frequently stalled on hard-to-verify infrastructure problems (especially PowerSync/offline sync), and Claude often produced correct diagnoses but non-working fixes while wrestling with repeated API output-token errors.

Unresolved sync/infrastructure debugging loops
A large share of your debugging sessions on PowerSync and offline-first sync ended with correct root-cause diagnoses but no working fix, because the real fault lived in external deploy/replication layers you couldn't fully verify in-session. You could shorten these loops by having Claude confirm the deployment/backfill state early and by isolating what's app-code versus platform behavior before cycling through fixes.
  • Multiple PowerSync sessions correctly isolated that non-_id ObjectIds replicate as null, yet the target org still synced 0 products at session end, leaving you without a usable result.
  • An Atlas trigger using aggregation-pipeline updateMany silently no-op'd in App Services, so the intended backfill never ran and debugging continued unproductively.
API output-token limit errors truncating work
Claude's responses repeatedly exceeded the 500 output-token maximum, producing API errors that truncated or entirely obscured sessions, making outcomes unrecoverable from the transcript. Breaking large tasks into smaller steps or requesting more concise responses would keep work visible and continuous.
  • Roughly a third of sessions were marked 'unclear_from_transcript' because captured responses were only token-limit API errors, so the actual work was lost.
  • Even in productive sessions, repeated token-limit errors interrupted the flow and forced restarts, adding friction to otherwise progressing tasks.
Wrong approach and interrupted redirections
Claude sometimes started with autonomous exploration or an inconsistent toolchain choice, prompting you to interrupt and re-issue requests to steer it back on track. Providing explicit constraints up front (e.g., which build tool, drawer direction, or lane ownership) would reduce these mid-course corrections.
  • Claude used electron-builder for the icon step after you had already switched to electron-forge, creating a config mismatch you had to catch and redirect.
  • You interrupted a standalone build and dashboard-redesign requests twice each, with the redesign transcript ending before any completed work was shown.

MCP Servers
Connect Claude directly to your MongoDB Atlas / PowerSync backend to query live sync state.
Why for you: Half your sessions were PowerSync debugging where the bottleneck was blind deploy-relaunch-log loops; a DB MCP server would let Claude inspect replicated rows and null fields directly instead of guessing.
claude mcp add mongodb -- npx -y @mongodb-js/mongodb-mcp-server --connectionString "$ATLAS_URI"
Custom Skills
Reusable one-command workflows defined as markdown.
Why for you: You repeatedly diagnose the same PowerSync null-ObjectId issue and run the same build-launch-verify Electron flow — a /sync-debug and /package skill would encode those steps once.
# .claude/skills/sync-debug/SKILL.md Check PowerSync sync-streams.yaml against AppSchema. Confirm no non-_id ObjectId fields are replicated (they become null). Verify orgKey denormalization. Query Atlas for row counts per org. Report zero-row orgs and likely cause.
Hooks
Auto-run shell commands at lifecycle events like after edits.
Why for you: You had 14 buggy-code frictions and TypeScript is your dominant language; an auto-typecheck hook after edits would catch collisions (like the i18n namespace clash) before you verify.
// .claude/settings.json { "hooks": { "PostToolUse": [{ "matcher": "Edit|Write", "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "pnpm typecheck"}] }] } }

Autonomous PowerSync Diagnostic Harness
Your logs show 8+ sessions cycling deploy-relaunch-log loops chasing null ObjectId replication, backfill completion, and stale bundle issues that consumed dozens of hours. An autonomous agent could own the entire diagnostic loop—instrumenting sync streams, replaying trigger backfills, polling client row counts, and iterating fixes until a target org syncs the expected rows without you babysitting each redeploy.
Getting started: Use a background Agent with Bash to run a scripted deploy-verify loop against PowerSync/Atlas, plus a status-poll assertion that gates completion on actual synced row counts.
Paste into Claude Code:
Build an autonomous PowerSync verification harness. Write a script that: (1) deploys sync-streams.yaml and any Atlas trigger changes, (2) triggers a backfill for a target orgKey, (3) polls the client sync status and product/customer row counts every 15s for up to 5 minutes, (4) asserts non-zero rows synced. Then run this loop autonomously: if rows are still 0, inspect connector logs for null-ObjectId replication, apply the next candidate fix (orgKey string denormalization, trigger updateMany scoping, re-replication), redeploy, and re-verify. Do NOT stop to ask me between iterations—only report back when rows sync successfully or after 6 failed fix attempts with a ranked hypothesis list.
